verses.note: The verse introduces the image of God: humanity made in God's image and likeness, with rule over the creatures as its first expression. Christian theology has read the image as reason, as royal representation, as relationship, or as a combination; the verse's own emphasis falls on representation and vocation.

Both male and female bear the image. The verse makes the image the possession of humanity as such, which the New Testament later grounds in Christ, the image of the invisible God into whose likeness believers are renewed (Colossians 1:15, 3:10).

Human life is protected because human beings bear God's image (Genesis 9:6). Jesus extended the command to anger and contempt (Matthew 5:21-22), treating it as a guard over the neighbor's worth, not only a ban on the final act.
The title ‘sons of God’ is given to those who share God's own work of reconciliation. Sonship here is shown in likeness: those who make peace resemble the God of peace.

By quoting Genesis 1:27, the verse on humanity made in God's image, Jesus ties the question of marriage to what human beings are. The difference and union of male and female belong to the created order that God called very good.

Adam is called ‘son of God’ because he was made in God's image and likeness (Genesis 5:1-3). The genealogy prepares for the New Testament's teaching that Jesus is the last Adam and the true image of God (1 Corinthians 15:45, Colossians 1:15).

The coin bears Caesar's image and belongs to him; human beings bear God's image (Genesis 1:27) and belong to God. Tertullian drew out this reading early (On Idolatry 15), and it remains the most natural way to hear the contrast between the two clauses.
Humanity, made in God's image, made images of creatures and worshiped them. The echo of Genesis 1 suggests that idolatry distorts the very thing that makes human beings human.

The image of God, damaged in the fall, is restored in the image of the Son. Humanity was made in God's image (Genesis 1:27); believers are being remade in the image of Christ, who is himself the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15).

Psalm 8 is a meditation on Genesis 1: humanity crowned to rule. By applying it to Christ, Paul shows that the vocation given to humanity at creation is fulfilled in him and, through him, in those who bear his likeness (verse 49).

Humanity bears the image of God (Genesis 1:26-27) but, as descendants of Adam, also bears Adam's image (Genesis 5:3). Paul says believers will bear the image of the heavenly man: the image of God, marred in Adam, will be fully restored in the likeness of the risen Christ.

By echoing Genesis 1:27, Paul ties the unity of the new humanity to the original creation in which both male and female bear God's image. The new creation restores rather than erases that shared dignity.

Humanity was made in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27); the Son is the image of God. Paul elsewhere says believers are renewed after the image of their Creator (3:10), so the Son is both the original of which humanity is a copy and the pattern to which it is restored.
